newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal pensions to rise in real terms in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Portugal pensions to rise in real terms in 1997.

text.p: Portuguese retirement pensions will rise by slightly more than inflation forecast for 1997 and the poorest retirees will receive more than the average increase, an official spokesman said on Thursday.
But he denied a report in Diario de Noticias newspaper that the government had decided to raise pensions by three percent next year and by 3.5 percent for the poorest retirees.

"The overall increase in pensions will be slightly over the forecast inflation rate for 1997 and the poorest will receive a bigger increase than the average," Antonio Ramos Andre of the Social Security Ministry told Reuters.
The Socialist government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has forecast that inflation in 1997 will be between 2.25 and 2.50 percent, down from 3.25 percent in 1996.
The poorest retirees in Portugal receive pensions of 20,000 escudos ($129) per month, Ramos Andre said.
The total cost of pensions is projected to rise by 6.3 percent to 1,095 billion escudos ($7.05 billion) in the 1997 budget proposals now being considered by parliament.
The increase takes into account the larger number of new pensioners entering the system than the number of deaths as the population ages in Portugal, Ramos Andre said.
It also incorporates the higher average pension paid to new pensioners than to those who die in a given year, as well as the percentage increase set by the government.
Parliament is expected to pass the budget in a vote on December 11.
"The increases in pensions will conform with the government's budget proposals," Ramos Andre said.
The government's budget proposals keep tight control of state spending in a bid to meet tough entry entry conditions for joining a single European currency in 1999.
Ramos Andre said his ministry expected to announce in November by how much retirement pensions would rise.
The 1997 pensions will be paid from December 1.
"We want to have as much information as possible before a final decision is taken," Ramos Andre said.
"By November the actual performance of the 1996 budget will be as complete as possible," he added.
